nc_cave_the.blurb: The largest section of Cathey's Creek Crag, a small Pisgah National Forest cliff set above a waterfall. The wall is steep and overhanging, which keeps it dry in a storm, and it sits in shade for most of the day. Climbing here is powerful and gymnastic. Most of the 16 lines are trad, with a few sport routes, spread from the upper 5.9 range through to the low 5.12s, and the bulk of them fall in the 5.11 band. It is a place for people comfortable on steep rock rather than a beginner's venue.

nc_left_of_main_southeast_face.blurb: A run of shorter walls to the left of the big southeast face on Whiteside Mountain, reached from the Whiteside trail parking. The climbing is all trad, mostly single pitch, and grades run from 5.8 up to the 5.12s, with most routes in the 5.11 range and a good handful at 5.10. The wall faces southeast like the main face and is said to drop into shade mid-afternoon in summer. Routes here tend to be quieter than the famous long lines nearby, and a standard rack is the norm.

nc_catwalk.blurb: A short cliff on the upper right side of Whiteside Mountain's north face, popular for summer cragging because the mountain is higher and cooler than its surroundings. It faces northwest and picks up some afternoon sun. Climbing is mostly single pitch, with crimpy face moves and the best lines being the shorter, harder ones. Of the 16 routes, roughly two thirds are trad and the rest sport, with grades from 5.8 into the low 5.13 range and the weight of the routes at 5.11 and 5.12. The walk in is a steep descent through a gully.

nc_flackamite_pirate_wall_the.blurb: A small wall in the Sitting Bear section of Linville Gorge, reached by the same trail as the main Sitting Bear routes and then a faint side path. It holds 16 routes, most of them trad, plus a few sport lines and a single boulder problem. Grades start near 5.7 and top out around 5.11, with most clustered between 5.10 and 5.11. Lines tend to be short, steep and technical, some with bolts and some wanting cams in pockets, and certain parts of the wall stay shaded and can be damp.

nc_01_practice_wall.blurb: The first wall most climbers meet on the trail at Crowders Mountain State Park near Gastonia, and one of the park's busiest spots, especially on fair weekends. It is known as a top-rope wall, with a two-bolt anchor for easy setups, although the lines include a crack, a seamed face and an arete that suit lead climbing too. Of the 15 routes, most are trad and a few top-rope, running from very easy up to the 5.14 range, with the largest group around 5.9 to 5.10. Hikers walk above the wall, so wear a helmet.

nc_test_pilots_buttress.blurb: A tall buttress at Rumbling Bald near Lake Lure, with steep face and crack lines. Almost everything is trad, with a single sport route, and the grades run from 5.8 into the 5.12s with most in the 5.10 to 5.11 range. Climbers can take the sunny side on cool, crisp days and switch to the shadier side for a pumpy workout when it warms up, which fits Rumbling Bald's reputation as a good fall and winter destination. It can be reached on the boulder-field path or on the Cereal Buttress trail.
